title: Why Go Beyond the Coursebook: The Case for Supplementary Materials
brief: Open this unit by establishing why teachers make and use their own materials. Draw on the module's framing of supplementary resources as 'practical, printable materials' that teachers can 'use or adapt to suit their teaching context and topics.' Emphasise the principle of adapting to local needs — the module repeatedly states that teachers should 'adopt or adapt teaching ideas to fit their local needs.' Introduce the idea that self-made materials are a normal, professional part of teaching, not a last resort, and that the unit will survey the main types a TEFL teacher can create at low cost.

title: Flashcards, Flip Books, and Pocket Books: Simple Visual Aids You Can Make
brief: Focus on three closely related DIY visual formats drawn directly from the module: flip books, and two types of pocket books ('What Do I See?' and 'The Book About Me'). The module states that flip book documents list 'materials and step-by-step instructions' and explain how flip books can be used. Pocket book documents explain how to make the books and include the materials needed; teachers can have students make their own copies by filling in the blanks. Explain how each format works as a teaching aid, what materials are typically required, and how students can participate in making them — reinforcing language through the creation process itself.

title: Puppets as Teaching Aids: Full-Sized, Hand, and Stick Puppets
brief: Cover the three puppet types described in the module: full-sized paper puppets, hand puppets, and stick puppets. The module notes that each type has its own document showing 'materials and step-by-step instructions.' For stick puppets specifically, the module mentions a template of a line drawing of a boy and girl 'that can be colored and cut out,' illustrating how a simple template reduces preparation time. Discuss how puppets function as classroom aids — giving a voice to characters, supporting storytelling, and encouraging student interaction — and connect puppet use to the module's broader point about making storytelling 'conversational so that students feel actively involved.'

title: Worksheets, Graphic Organizers, and Assessment Tools
brief: Draw on the module's descriptions of printable worksheet resources: the vocabulary assessment worksheet that 'includes a rubric and visual cues' for very young learners, the graphic organizer for brainstorming that 'can be reproduced on the board during class,' and the self- and peer-assessment checklist used in the writing activity where 'students use a checklist to assess their own writing and also to assess the writing of a classmate.' Show how each of these represents a different function — practice, planning support, and assessment — and explain that teachers can create similar tools themselves by following the same principles: clear visual layout, adaptable content, and a defined task for the student.

title: Realia and Mixed Media: Using Everyday Objects and Recycled Materials
brief: Draw entirely on the Create to Communicate source material to explain how everyday and recycled materials become powerful teaching aids. The module lists recycled materials that can be used in art-based language activities: 'cardboard, shoe boxes, cereal boxes, brown paper bags, recycled papers and magazines, glass and plastic jars.' It also lists materials from nature — 'grass, straw, twigs, sand, small rocks, leaves' — as optional mixed media components. The module states that 'teachers may collect some from personal belongings or ask students to bring in recycled materials,' making this a genuinely low-cost approach. Explain how combining materials (collage plus drawing, paint plus collage elements, bookmaking with drawings inside) gives students 'many avenues for expression, exploration, and experimentation while using English.'

title: Putting It All Together: Choosing and Using Aids Effectively in Your Lessons
brief: Synthesise the unit by helping teachers decide when and how to deploy the aids covered. Draw on the module's action-plan prompts, which ask teachers to consider questions such as how they will 'support vocabulary development and student interaction,' what 'follow-up activities' to include, and what 'classroom management techniques may be required.' Reference the module's point about signal words — using a special word or gesture to mark transitions — as an example of a simple, non-material aid that structures activity around physical resources. Close by reinforcing the module's cycle of 'adopt or adapt': teachers should try a self-made aid, reflect on what worked, and revise for next time, treating material-making as an ongoing professional practice rather than a one-off task.
